Question
========
Using AVX2 or CUDA as you prefer, write a cache-aligned matrix multiplication, as done in phase 4 of the project.

Solution
========
An AVX2 version, assuming square matrices of float of size n, n a multiple of 8, and all three matrices allocated 32-byte aligned with `aligned_alloc` or `_mm_malloc`:

    // Assumes n % 8 == 0 and A, B, C are 32-byte aligned.
    // B is accessed row-wise so that the inner loop is contiguous.
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j += 8)
            _mm256_store_ps(&C[i*n + j], _mm256_setzero_ps());
        for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
            __m256 a = _mm256_set1_ps(A[i*n + k]);   // broadcast one scalar
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j += 8) {
                __m256 b = _mm256_load_ps(&B[k*n + j]);
                __m256 c = _mm256_load_ps(&C[i*n + j]);
                c = _mm256_fmadd_ps(a, b, c);        // c += a * b
                _mm256_store_ps(&C[i*n + j], c);
            }
        }
    }

The points that matter: the loop order is i, k, j and not i, j, k, so that the innermost loop walks a row of B and a row of C contiguously instead of striding down a column of B; the scalar of A is broadcast once per k; aligned load and store are used rather than the unaligned variants, which is what the alignment buys; and the accumulation happens in a vector register.

A blocked version, tiling i, j and k so that a tile of B stays in L1, is the next step and is what actually gives the large speedup on big matrices.
